title: Amir Ali OBE — Remote Court Users: debt recovery and 'the NHS for the law'
pub: Legally Speaking podcast (LegalTechTalk Uncovered miniseries, London)
author: Amir Ali

dom.t: Neglected claims: AI services target uneconomic legal work

st.t: Neglected claims: AI services target uneconomic legal work
st.an: Ali supports the cluster’s diagnosis that business debt recovery is underserved, slow and cumbersome. However, he offers neither a specific AI solution nor evidence on bounded workflows, low-price delivery, accuracy, recovery outcomes or scalable economics, so his position on the cluster’s principal AI-services proposition cannot be determined.

kp.k: Business debt recovery remains slow and underserved
kp.d: Ali argues that, although lawyers serve businesses well in other areas, debt recovery, dispute resolution and litigation inadequately serve businesses owed money for services rendered. This is his diagnosis of the problem Remote Court Users seeks to address, rather than a measured finding.
qs: the legal profession are very good at servicing the business community in all aspects of what they do, in all areas of what they do.
uh the system is slow, it's clunky, and  that's what I'm going to try and resolve.

kp.k: Professional resistance impedes affordable, timely legal services
kp.d: Ali challenges the assumption that human-delivered legal services can readily provide quick, cheap and fair solutions. He attributes resistance to change to the profession's human organisation, risk aversion and monopoly; the transcript supplies no comparative evidence for this assessment.
qs: The fact that they think there is a  solution out there that a human can deal with quickly and cheaply and fairly. But it doesn't work like that.
The legal profession is it's it's run by humans. It's risk averse. They don't like change and they have a monopoly.

kp.k: Judgment transfers anchor a newly launched recovery service
kp.d: Speaking in 2025, Ali says Remote Court Users launched earlier that year following development of the idea during the pandemic. Its core offering transfers county court judgments to the High Court for enforcement, enabling involvement of a high court enforcement officer. The proposed service restructuring concerns debt recovery and court processes, not a specified AI application.
qs: we've only just launched remote court users uh earlier on this year
a core business offering, core service offering which is transferring a county court judgment to the high court and going to then enforce that uh in the high court.
the  county court judgment can then be transferred to the high court and then you can get a high court enforcement officer involved.

kp.k: Unawareness allegedly leaves 650,000 eligible applications untapped
kp.d: Ali reports approximately 120,000 annual applications and says Remote Court Users has identified a further 650,000 annually meeting the transfer criteria. He attributes this untapped volume to judgment holders not knowing the mechanism exists and says his organisation will help for free. These are his organisation's claims; the transcript does not explain its identification methodology or the scope of the free assistance.
qs: Now currently there are 120 odd,000 applications a year that go to court.
remote court users has identified  over a number of years uh that there are a further 650,000 applications a year that meet the criteria that could be fed into the system.
they're getting the judgments, but because they don't know that this system exists.
We're here to help and actually we'll do it for free.

kp.k: Digitisation conditions projected growth in court fee income
kp.d: Ali estimates that the existing application stream generates around £8 million annually for the Ministry of Justice and HMCTS, and argues that expanded use could increase this to £54 million. He says he is working with those bodies to try to digitise the process, presenting digitisation as necessary to handle the volume. The revenue increase is a projection, not a reported outcome, and no AI system is described.
qs: There is a court fee to pay for each of those applications.
So circa the Ministry of Justice and HMCTS get around8 million pounds a year from that one application.
you could increase your fee income from this one application from 8 million to 54 million.

one of the things we  are doing uh with uh the ministry of justice and his majesty's courts and tribunal service the court service is to try and digitize that because the only way we can deal with this is to digitize it.

kp.k: Recovery profits would cross-subsidise public legal advice
kp.d: Ali describes Remote Court Users as a nonprofit and sets out an intended allocation of profits: 10% to staff, 20% retained and 70% to a foundation. He links retention to his ambition for the organisation to specialise exclusively in judgment transfers and recovery through the High Court. The interview presents this funding structure as the organisation's direction of travel, without reporting distributions or financial results.
qs: It is a non for profofit. 10% of the profits will be paid to the staff. 20% will be retained
I want it to be the only organization to do this one thing and one thing well i.e. transfer county court judgments to the high court
70% of the profits of that company um will be paid in uh will be paid into a BC Corp  certified foundation.

kp.k: Legal Aid Foundation aims for free legal access
kp.d: Ali's proposed Legal Aid Foundation would advise people unable to afford legal help. He reports that three former Supreme Court judges have agreed to lead it, with trustees drawn from the bench helping write its rules. His analogy is the NHS: legal assistance free at the point of contact. This is an access-to-justice ambition financed through the recovery service, not evidence of an operating universal service or AI-enabled delivery.

there'll be a plethora of trustees. All of them come from the bench.
they will help me write the rules and regulations.
it'll have one job and one job only and that is to offer legal advice to  everybody in society that can't afford it.
the name of the foundation is uh and we've already secured the name and the domain names will be the Legal Aid Foundation.
You're in the system, looked after for free because it's free at the point of contact. It's called the NHS.
my vision and ambition for uh the legal aid foundation is for it to be the NHS for the law.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Amir Ali makes no concrete AI-specific claim. His relevant claims concern digitising judgment enforcement and using its proceeds to fund legal advice.
pts.d: Ali describes business debt recovery as slow and poorly served. He claims Remote Court Users has identified substantial unused capacity to transfer county court judgments to the High Court for enforcement, and argues that digitisation is necessary to handle that volume. He projects that additional applications could increase annual court-fee income from approximately £8 million to £54 million. Separately, he proposes allocating 70% of the organisation's profits to a Legal Aid Foundation offering advice to people unable to afford it. These are digitisation and service-funding claims, not claims about AI automation or AI replacing lawyers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Ali offers internally identified application volumes and professional experience, rather than AI evidence or demonstrated service outcomes.
pts.d: Ali reports approximately 120,000 existing transfer applications annually, generating roughly £8 million in court fees, and a further 650,000 eligible applications identified by Remote Court Users over several years. He provides no underlying dataset or identification methodology. His experience includes 21 years as a lawyer, approximately 13 years in High Court enforcement, and 11 years on the Civil Court Users Association board. He also reports discussions with government and judicial commitments to the proposed foundation. These support his account of the initiative's background; the interview supplies no measured digitisation results, AI benchmarks, or evidence that the proposed foundation is already delivering advice.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The service had launched earlier in 2025; digitisation, expanded application volumes, and foundation-funded advice remain plans without specified completion dates.
pts.d: In this 2025 interview, Ali says the initiative's thought process developed during the pandemic and Remote Court Users launched earlier that year. He describes ongoing efforts with the Ministry of Justice and HMCTS to digitise the transfer process. The application and revenue figures are annual estimates, not achieved increases. Expansion depends on reaching eligible judgment creditors and processing additional applications. The foundation's funding depends on Remote Court Users generating profits and allocating the proposed 70% share. Ali gives no deadline for achieving the projected scale or the foundation's access-to-justice ambition.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The proposed beneficiaries are business judgment creditors, the court service, and people unable to afford legal advice.
pts.d: Ali targets businesses across sectors that have obtained judgments but do not know about the High Court enforcement route; he says Remote Court Users will help them for free, while separately noting that transfer applications carry a court fee. The Ministry of Justice and HMCTS would receive additional fee income if application volumes increase. High Court enforcement officers would become involved in collecting qualifying debts. The proposed foundation would address unmet legal need among people unable to afford advice, distinct from the business debt-recovery service. Ali also proposes distributing 10% of profits to staff and retaining 20% within the organisation.
